title: food as practice
hook: a proud student is told to stop eating, and his father's lesson arrives as an ember

segments.voice: Last time, food as practice, and a knock at the door: make much food, turn no one away. Did some of the extra find its way to someone else? Day one thousand three hundred twelve.

A student comes home after years of study, sure of himself, full of verses. His father decides to test him, and the test isn't a debate. It's a diet. Eat nothing for a while, the father says. Drink all the water you like. Then come back and recite what you know. The student is Shvetaketu. The father is Uddalaka. The experiment sits in the sixth chapter of the Chandogya Upanishad. Today: what a meal has to do with a mind.
screen: `A STUDENT HOME, SURE OF HIMSELF.` → `THE TEST IS A DIET.` → `WHAT A MEAL HAS TO DO WITH A MIND.`

segments.voice: It starts with a claim, here in paraphrase. Food, once eaten, divides three ways. The coarsest part leaves the body. The middle part becomes flesh. The finest part becomes mind. Then Uddalaka puts it in one line, which in Sanskrit runs annamayam hi somya manah: the mind, my dear, is made of food. Water, he adds, becomes breath, and heat becomes speech. Then the test. The text says fifteen days without food, with water allowed. Shvetaketu comes back, and his father asks for the verses he spent all those years learning. They don't come to me, sir, he says. So Uddalaka gives him a picture. A great fire has burned down to one ember, the size of a firefly. It can't burn much now. Add straw, and it blazes again. Go and eat, his father says. Shvetaketu eats, comes back, and the verses are all there. And he understood, the text says. Three things sit inside that story. First, it's humbling. The young scholar who thought learning lived somewhere above the body finds it leaning on lunch. Second, it's kind to the body. The Upanishad doesn't scold anyone for needing to eat. It treats the plate as part of how a person thinks. Third, it's a doorway. This is the same chapter where Uddalaka will later say tat tvam asi, that thou art. He is teaching his son what a self is, and food is one of the first things he reaches for. And a plain word, since these days hold Ayurveda to a careful standard: this is a teaching story, not a fasting plan, and nobody should copy the experiment. What it offers is a way to see a meal. Not fuel poured in while the real you is somewhere else, but an ember being fed.
screen: `FOOD DIVIDES THREE WAYS` · `THE MIND, MY DEAR, IS MADE OF FOOD` · `AN EMBER THE SIZE OF A FIREFLY` · `A TEACHING STORY, NOT A FASTING PLAN`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: tend the ember. Sit comfortably and let the breath settle. Rest a hand low on the belly, if you like, and feel any warmth there. Then let a small ember come to mind, glowing, about the size of a firefly. With each breath in, let it brighten a little, the way a coal brightens when air reaches it. With each breath out, let it settle and glow. Nothing to fix, nothing to earn. If the mind wanders, come back to the ember. If you pray, you can give thanks for the food that is holding you up in this moment. The bell holds the time.
Food as practice. In the Chandogya, the finest part of a meal becomes mind, and a hungry student's verses come back after he eats. Today's word.
Your line: food as practice. Today, before you eat, take one breath and remember the ember: this plate is about to become part of how you think. Day one thousand three hundred twelve.

howItsDone: Some Hindus fast on particular days as a devotional practice, while teachers of the Upanishads read Uddalaka's experiment as a lesson about the self, not as a fasting rule.

fork.setup: you're Uddalaka. your son has fasted, and now he can't recall the verses he learned. what do you do?
options: send him back to study them again.
tell him to go and eat, then ask again.
tell him the verses never mattered.
fork.reveal: he gives him the ember, a coal the size of a firefly that blazes with straw, and sends him to eat. the verses come back, and Shvetaketu understands.

original.note: Sanskrit, Chandogya Upanishad 6.5.4: the mind, my dear, is made of food. anna is food; manas is mind.

trapdoor: what you thought: food is fuel for the body, and the mind lives somewhere else.
what it means: in the Chandogya, the finest part of food becomes mind, and a hungry student can't recall his verses.
what a scholar hears: Uddalaka's firefly-sized ember, in the same chapter that later says tat tvam asi, that thou art.

sources.ref: Chandogya Upanishad 6.1.1–3 (Shvetaketu returns from study, proud)
Chandogya Upanishad 6.5.1–4 (food divides three ways; the mind is made of food, breath of water, speech of heat)
Chandogya Upanishad 6.7.1–6 (fifteen days without food, water allowed; the ember the size of a firefly; he eats and remembers)

notes: Review picks up day 1311 (Taittiriya 3.10, the guest). Days 1307–1311 used Bhrigu, measure, Charaka's method of eating, Gita 17's three foods and the guest; this day's Chandogya 6.5–6.7 angle is new.

Chandogya 6.5: confirm the threefold division (coarsest, middle, finest) for food and the summary line 'annamayam hi somya manah, apomayah pranah, tejomayi vak'; Devanagari of the original line to be checked.

Chandogya 6.7: 'fifteen days' and 'water as you like' are in 6.7.1; the firefly-sized ember and the straw in 6.7.3–5; Shvetaketu's reply that the verses do not occur to him in 6.7.2. Confirm the paraphrase.
Science-seat line: the lesson says plainly this is a teaching story, not a fasting plan, and should not be copied.
